title: A* priority
parameters: g is cost already incurred, h estimates remaining cost, f estimates total cost via n.
purpose: Rank pending routes by estimated total path cost.
assumptions: Use smallest f on OPEN; update g when a better route arrives.
example: g=4 and h=3 give f=7.
variation: h=0 reduces to uniform-cost search. Greedy uses h alone.
mistake: Using the number of edges for g when edge costs differ.
recall: If g=5 and h=4, what is f?

title: Heuristic bounds
parameters: h* is the true remaining cost and c is the arc cost.
purpose: Admissibility is a bound per node.
assumptions: Admissibility is a bound per node. Consistency checks each arc and h(goal)=0.
example: An arc of cost 2 from h=7 to h=4 violates consistency because 7>6.
variation: A consistent heuristic with zero at goals is admissible for reachable goals.
mistake: Checking only the overall start and goal values.
recall: c=2 and h(child)=4. What is the maximum consistent h(parent) on this edge?

title: Minimax value
parameters: U is terminal utility measured from MAX’s perspective and n_i are legal children.
purpose: Perfect-information, two-player zero-sum deterministic game.
assumptions: Perfect-information, two-player zero-sum deterministic game. Replace U with an evaluation at cutoff if depth-limited.
example: A MIN node with leaves 5 and 9 backs up 5.
variation: A chance node in expectiminimax uses expected utility.
mistake: Comparing all leaves without respecting who controls each transition.
recall: MIN faces values 4, 9 and −2. What value is backed up?

title: Alpha–beta cutoff
parameters: Alpha is the lower bound established by MAX and beta the upper bound established by MIN.
purpose: Keep both bounds for depth-first minimax.
assumptions: Keep both bounds for depth-first minimax. Update alpha at MAX and beta at MIN.
example: Inherited α=5, new β=3 after a MIN leaf: remaining children can be skipped.
variation: Visit promising moves early for more cutoffs.
mistake: Resetting inherited bounds at each node.
recall: If α=5, how large can β be and still cause a cutoff?

title: Support, confidence and lift
parameters: N is the number of transactions and n(S) counts transactions containing S.
purpose: Use disjoint nonempty antecedent and consequent.
assumptions: Use disjoint nonempty antecedent and consequent. Know whether minsup is a proportion or count.
example: For n(XY)=6,n(X)=8,n(Y)=10,N=20, support=.30, confidence=.75, lift=1.5.
variation: Reverse the rule to change confidence. Lift remains symmetric.
mistake: Using antecedent support as the lift denominator.
recall: Of 10 transactions, 4 contain A and 3 contain both A and B. What is confidence A→B?

title: Antimonotone support
parameters: X is a subset of itemset Y and n counts containing transactions.
purpose: Use to prune Apriori candidates when a required subset is infrequent.
assumptions: Use to prune Apriori candidates when a required subset is infrequent.
example: If n(AB)=2 < 3, then n(ABC)≤2 and ABC is infrequent.
variation: Join compatible frequent sets before checking their remaining immediate subsets.
mistake: Treating a surviving candidate as frequent before a support scan.
recall: AB has support count 2. What is the largest possible support count of ABC?

title: Entropy, information gain and Gini
expression: H(D)=-\sum_c p_c\log_2 p_c,\quad IG=H(D)-\sum_j\frac{\lvert D_j\rvert }{\lvert D\rvert }H(D_j),\quad G=1-\sum_c p_c^2
parameters: p_c is the fraction of class c in the current node. D_j is a child partition.
purpose: Apply 0 log 0=0 and weight by child size.
assumptions: Apply 0 log 0=0 and weight by child size. Higher gain means a greater entropy decrease.
example: A 50–50 node has entropy 1 bit and Gini .5.
variation: Gain ratio divides information gain by entropy of the child-size fractions when nonzero.
mistake: Using parent class fractions when evaluating a child.
recall: A binary node is pure. What is its Gini impurity?

title: Confusion-matrix rates
parameters: TP, FP, TN and FN are counts relative to the chosen positive class.
purpose: Check denominators are nonzero.
assumptions: Check denominators are nonzero. TPR is sensitivity and 1−FPR is specificity.
example: TP=12,FN=8,FP=10,TN=70 gives TPR=.6, FPR=.125, precision=12/22.
variation: ROC plots TPR versus FPR across thresholds. Accuracy divides total correct by all predictions.
mistake: Using predicted positives as the denominator for sensitivity.
recall: TP=12 and FN=8. What is recall?

title: Minkowski and cosine measures
parameters: x,z are coordinate vectors, r≥1, and both norms must be nonzero for cosine.
purpose: For r=1 use absolute sum.
assumptions: For r=1 use absolute sum; for r=2 use Euclidean. r→∞ gives maximum coordinate difference.
example: (0,0) to (3,4) gives Euclidean 5 and L∞ 4.
variation: Cosine compares direction, so shared positive scaling leaves it unchanged.
mistake: Forgetting absolute values in L1 or the square root in Euclidean.
recall: What is the Euclidean distance between (1,3) and (4,7)?

source.file: Lecture/Topic5_IE4483-EE6483 Nearest Neighbor Classifiers and Support Vector Machines.pdf

title: Canonical hard margin
parameters: x_i is a feature vector, y_i=±1, w is the normal, b is the intercept.
purpose: Compute the geometric separation of canonical support planes.
assumptions: For separable data with canonical ±1 support levels. Distance from boundary to a support plane is half the width.
example: Points 2 and 6 give w=.5,b=−2, boundary 4 and width 4.
variation: At levels ±a the width formula is 2a/‖w‖.
mistake: Applying 2/‖w‖ after arbitrary rescaling without rescaling support levels.
recall: In canonical form with ‖w‖=4, what is the full width?

source.file: Lecture/Topic5_IE4483-EE6483 Nearest Neighbor Classifiers and Support Vector Machines.pdf

title: Minimum slack
parameters: ξ is the smallest nonnegative violation and y_i is the signed training label.
purpose: Use on the soft margin.
assumptions: Use on the soft margin. Check the signed score to distinguish violations from classification errors.
example: A signed score .2 gives slack .8 while the prediction is correct.
variation: A squared slack penalty penalizes large violations differently from hinge loss.
mistake: Treating every positive slack as a wrong class.
recall: If the signed score is −.25, what is minimum slack?

source.file: Lecture/Topic5_IE4483-EE6483 Nearest Neighbor Classifiers and Support Vector Machines.pdf

title: Bayesian posterior
parameters: H_j partition the possibilities and E is the observed evidence.
purpose: The evidence must have positive total probability.
assumptions: The evidence must have positive total probability.
example: P(A)=.2, likelihoods .6 and .3 give posterior .12/.36=1/3.
variation: When choosing MAP, compare the numerators because the denominator is shared.
mistake: Inverting likelihood without priors and normalization.
recall: Two exclusive, exhaustive hypotheses are equally likely before the observation. The observation has likelihood 0.6 under the first and 0.2 under the second. What is the posterior probability of the first?

title: Naïve Bayes score
parameters: c indexes class labels and x_j are observed feature values.
purpose: The model assumes conditional independence given each class.
assumptions: The model assumes conditional independence given each class. Apply declared smoothing or raw counts.
example: Scores .12 and .03 normalize to .80 and .20.
variation: Take log scores for robust MAP ranking with many features.
mistake: Omitting observed zeros or multiplying marginal feature probabilities.
recall: Two class scores are .12 and .03. What is the first posterior?

title: Unit activation
parameters: w_ji connects upstream unit i to j, o_i is its output, b_j is bias and G is activation.
purpose: Use the given activation at every unit, then pass outputs to later units.
assumptions: Use the given activation at every unit, then pass outputs to later units.
example: w=(.5,1), x=(2,−1), b=.4 gives net=.4 and ReLU output .4.
variation: An explicit constant input 1 allows a bias to be represented as its weight.
mistake: Feeding a pre-activation forward without applying the nonlinearity.
recall: What is ReLU(−3)?

title: Squared-loss backpropagation
parameters: k are downstream units, j is hidden, t are targets and δ uses the lecture’s negative-gradient convention.
purpose: Compute the derivative at the pre-activation.
assumptions: Compute the derivative at the pre-activation. For ReLU use 1 on positives and 0 on negatives; declare a convention at zero.
example: Active linear/ReLU output .6 with target .2 gives δ=−.4.
variation: A sigmoid derivative equals o(1−o). Other losses can change the output formula.
mistake: Using incoming weights in the hidden error term.
recall: For E = ½(t−o)² with this course’s convention δ = −∂E/∂net, an active output has o = 0.6, t = 0.2, and local derivative 1. What is δ?

title: Weight and bias updates
parameters: η is learning rate, δ_j is the negative-derivative error signal and o_i is the input activation.
purpose: Add these increments for the lecture’s delta sign.
assumptions: Add these increments for the lecture’s delta sign. Compute deltas using pre-update weights.
example: η=.2, δ=.5 and o_i=.3 gives Δw=.03 and Δb=.1.
variation: In gradient notation subtract η∇E instead.
mistake: Using the downstream unit’s activation in the incoming weight update.
recall: η=.1, δ=.4, input .5. What is Δw?

title: Gradient descent
parameters: θ denotes parameters, η the positive step size and E the objective.
purpose: Evaluate the gradient at the current parameters.
assumptions: Evaluate the gradient at the current parameters; the mini-batch version estimates it from the batch.
example: θ=2, slope=3, η=.1 yields 1.7.
variation: SGD uses one example per update in the lecture’s convention.
mistake: Increasing η indiscriminately can cause overshoot or divergence.
recall: Current θ=3, derivative −2 and η=.1. What is the new θ?

title: Convolution output dimensions
parameters: I is one input dimension, F its filter extent, P symmetric padding, S stride and K filters.
purpose: Dilation 1, integer stride, and at least one valid window.
assumptions: Dilation 1, integer stride, and at least one valid window. Apply independently along each axis.
example: I=10,F=3,P=1,S=2 gives O=5.
variation: Valid padding sets P=0; an odd filter with P=(F−1)/2 preserves size at stride 1.
mistake: Omitting the floor or final +1.
recall: A one-dimensional input of length I=9 uses a filter of width F=3, padding P=0, stride S=2 and dilation 1. What is output length O?

title: Convolution parameter count
parameters: F_h,F_w are spatial filter size, C_in is input channels and K is filter count.
purpose: For standard dense convolution with one bias per filter.
assumptions: For standard dense convolution with one bias per filter.
example: With six 5×5 RGB filters the count is 6(75+1)=456.
variation: Omit +1 if biases are disabled. Standard pooling has zero learned parameters.
mistake: Multiplying weights by spatial output locations.
recall: Four 3×3 filters with two input channels and bias. How many parameters?

title: Squared-error decomposition
parameters: Expectation covers random training sets and independent test noise at x. σ² is conditional noise variance.
purpose: Use for a fixed input with squared loss, independent train/test noise and zero-mean residual noise conditional on x.
assumptions: Use for a fixed input with squared loss, independent train/test noise and zero-mean residual noise conditional on x.
example: Bias .2, variance .03 and noise .10 yield expected squared error .17.
variation: Curves give practical diagnostics without measuring each term directly.
mistake: Assuming a smaller generalization gap alone means a better model.
recall: Bias .3, variance .02, noise .01. What is the expected squared error?

title: K-means centroid and objective
parameters: C_k is the set of samples in cluster k and μ_k its centroid.
purpose: Use Euclidean assignment then recompute nonempty cluster means.
assumptions: Use Euclidean assignment then recompute nonempty cluster means; define tie and empty-cluster policy.
example: Cluster {2,4,9} has centroid 5 and SSE 9+1+16=26.
variation: For L1 objective, medians replace means coordinatewise.
mistake: Changing one centroid during the assignment pass changes Lloyd’s algorithm.
recall: What is the centroid of 1, 2 and 9?

title: Single, complete and average linkage
parameters: a∈A and b∈B range over all cross-cluster pairs.
purpose: Apply the named linkage after each HAC merge.
assumptions: Apply the named linkage after each HAC merge.
example: {0,2} versus {6,7} gives 4, 7 and 5.5 respectively.
variation: Average-link distances can be updated with a size-weighted mean of earlier distances.
mistake: Dividing by \lvert A\rvert +\lvert B\rvert  instead of \lvert A\rvert \lvert B\rvert .
recall: Cross-pair distances are 2,4,6,8. What is average linkage?

title: Covariance and eigenvalues
parameters: N is number of samples, μ is the mean, S is covariance and λ_j is variance along unit u_j.
purpose: Center data first.
assumptions: Center data first. Use 1/(N−1) when sample covariance is required.
example: S=diag(4,1) gives first direction (1,0) up to sign.
variation: Changing covariance normalization scales eigenvalues but preserves directions when only the scalar factor changes.
mistake: Centering across features within each sample instead of across samples for each feature.
recall: For S=diag(4,1), what is the largest eigenvalue?

title: Projection and reconstruction
parameters: Columns of U are the k kept unit principal directions and R_k is retained variance fraction.
purpose: Encode centered observations and reconstruct approximate original coordinates.
assumptions: Use the training mean and scaling for new samples; positive total variance is required for the ratio.
variation: If the basis vector’s sign is flipped, so is the score; reconstruction is unchanged.
mistake: Leaving the reconstructed sample in centered coordinates.
recall: Eigenvalues 6,3,1. What variance fraction do the first two components retain?

title: Least-squares line
expression: \hat y=mx+b,\quad m=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2},\quad b=\bar y-m\bar x
parameters: x is the predictor, y the response and bars are sample means.
purpose: Fit a line that minimizes vertical squared residuals.
assumptions: Use the solution with an intercept for nonconstant predictor x.
example: Points (0,1),(1,3),(2,5) give m=2 and b=1.
variation: Use a design matrix for multiple linear features. A no-intercept fit uses different normal equations.
mistake: Minimizing perpendicular residuals or ignoring the intercept.
recall: m=2, x̄=3 and ȳ=5. What is b?
